question: How can an LLM inference engine adapt parallelism, precision, kernels, memory, caching, scheduling and communication at runtime to hold throughput and latency under varying load?
hypothesis: A static one-size-fits-all serving configuration is no longer sufficient; runtime-adaptive strategies outperform it.
contributions: Survey/practice guide of dynamic parallelism switching, dynamic precision, kernel autotuning, occupancy-aware shared memory, speculative KV prefetching, KV compression and policy switching, RL tuning, allocator switching, kernel hot-swap, CUDA Graph prewarming, adaptive batching and chunked prefill, congestion/topology-aware NVLink scheduling, MoE rebalancing

practices: Run multiple presharded model instances (TP-only for short latency-sensitive requests, TP+PP for long prompts) and route per request; do not reshard on the fly (Adaptive Parallelism).
Use the lowest precision that holds accuracy and fall back to higher precision when confidence drops; calibrate entropy/margin thresholds on a validation set with hysteresis (Dynamic Precision).

Prefer BF16 over FP16 for latency-critical decode on Blackwell; use Transformer Engine MXFP8 for FP8 and NVFP4 selectively for KV cache and light layers, since torch.autocast covers only FP16/BF16 (Dynamic Precision).
Warm up kernels at model load across extreme batch sizes and sequence lengths, cache the autotuned kernel choice keyed by workload signature (Kernel Autotuning).
Prefetch KV one layer ahead on a separate CUDA stream with pinned host buffers, and sync with events only at handoff; measure TTFT with NVTX (Speculative KV Prefetching).
Use HF cache_implementation='offloaded' as low-effort KV offload default; expect ~5-10% lower tokens/s (KV Prefetching).

Compress KV by quantization first; keep a recent full-precision window; trigger 8-bit above ~80% GPU memory and 4-bit under extreme pressure; add hysteresis and cooldown; swap policy at safe points (KV Compression).
Start with heuristics and add an RL agent only when stable; constrain actions, use soft latency-penalty reward, damping, shadow mode and a kill switch (RL Agents).
Separate long-lived allocations (weights) from short-lived (token buffers); consider cudaMallocAsync; always have an OOM fallback tier (Memory Allocation Switching).
Hot-swap kernels only behind feature flags, canary traffic and equivalence tests, with rollback if not faster on live data (Runtime Kernel Patching).
Prewarm CUDA Graph pools for common batch sizes using time-series forecasts (ARIMA, Prophet), on low-priority streams, and warm new instances before adding to traffic (Continuous Prewarming).

Treat prefill and decode as separate queues; serve decode first; chunk long prefills so a chunk takes ~50-100 ms; bucket prompts by length (~512-token buckets) (Adaptive Batching and Chunked Prefill).
Use homogeneous prefill/decode nodes unless the prefill:decode ratio is predictable (Adaptive Batching).

For small latency-sensitive reductions use tree all-reduce, for very large messages ring; stagger large collectives in waves; 2-4 simultaneous large transfers is the stated sweet spot (Congestion-Aware Scheduling).
